elements.quote: Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses on diabetes and COVID19 prognosis have observed an approximately two- to threefold increased risk of mortality due to COVID-19 for people with diabetes compared with people without diabetes [6 - 14]. However, diabetes is a complex and heterogeneous disease and recent studies have found that there are differences in associations of specific phenotypes of diabetes with comorbidities and complications [15]. ... However, some of the findings are still conflicting, imprecisely estimated or affected by risk of bias, such as confounding.
elements.reason: The Introduction describes current knowledge (diabetes as risk factor for poor COVID-19 prognosis) and key uncertainties (conflicting, imprecise findings, risk of bias, phenotype-level knowledge gaps).

elements.quote: Thus, findings from single studies are difficult to translate to clinical practice. To provide the best available evidence for the identification of risk phenotypes of diabetes in association with COVID-19 severity and death, a systematic review and meta-analysis is needed that summarises the findings, reveals more robust estimates, considers risk of bias and evaluates the certainty of evidence.
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are explicitly stated, including the rationale that a meta-analysis is needed for robust estimates and certainty evaluation.

elements.quote: Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses on diabetes and COVID19 prognosis have observed an approximately two- to threefold increased risk of mortality due to COVID-19 for people with diabetes compared with people without diabetes [6 - 14].
elements.reason: Previous similar systematic reviews are identified and cited, and the Introduction implies these did not address diabetes phenotypes specifically; however, the need for the new review relative to these prior reviews is only implicitly (not explicitly) explained.
This is a prognostic review of risk phenotypes, not a review of intervention effects, so a mechanism-of-action description is not required.
This is not a review of complex interventions or delivery contexts; no logic model requirement applies.

elements.quote: The aim of this study is to identify high-risk phenotypes of diabetes associated with COVID-19 severity and death.
elements.reason: The objective is explicitly stated in the abstract's Aims/hypothesis section, and reinforced in the introduction: 'we are conducting a living systematic review and meta-analysis on the associations between phenotypes of diabetes and confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with relation to COVID-19 death and severity' (callout_0).

elements.quote: a living systematic review and meta-analysis on the associations between phenotypes of diabetes and confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with relation to COVID-19 death and severity
elements.reason: This is a review of prognostic/risk factor associations in observational studies, not a review of intervention effects, so PICO-formatted planned comparisons do not apply.

elements.quote: We included studies of any design that reported risk estimates (HR, RR or OR with 95% CI) for associations between phenotypes (general characteristics of individuals, diabetes-specific characteristics, presence of diabetes-related complications or underlying comorbidities, and laboratory parameters) and death and severity of COVID-19 in individuals with diabetes and WHO-defined confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection [20]. Severity of COVID-19 was defined as a composite endpoint, including death, endotracheal intubation for mechanical ventilation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, ICU admission, multiple organ dysfunction or failure, or hospital admission.
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria specify population (individuals with diabetes and confirmed SARS-CoV-2), exposures (phenotypes), outcomes (death and severity with definitions), and eligible study designs (any design reporting risk estimates).

elements.quote: Studies without primary clinical data (including modelling studies), editorials, letters, commentaries, reviews, articles not in English and guidelines were excluded.
elements.reason: Report characteristics are specified: publication status/type (primary clinical data required; editorials, letters, commentaries, reviews, guidelines excluded) and language restriction (English only).

elements.quote: We successfully contacted study authors and received missing data or corrections for implausible data [16, 17, 24 - 27] and, thus, no study had to be excluded due to missing data.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states no study was excluded due to missing data, so the distinction between unmeasured and unreported outcomes does not arise.

elements.quote: For similar exposures (with similar reference groups [e.g., men vs women; obese vs normal weight; use of insulin: yes vs no; pre-existing comorbidities: yes vs no]), meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes: death and severity.
elements.reason: Synthesis groups are specified: meta-analyses stratified by exposure categories with defined reference groups and conducted separately for the two outcomes (death and severity) defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: Studies with mixed populations (including individuals without diabetes or without COVID-19) were excluded [21 - 23].
elements.reason: Some restrictions are implicitly justified (e.g., excluding mixed populations to focus on individuals with diabetes and COVID-19; excluding non-English articles), but explicit rationales for notable restrictions such as the English-language limit are not provided.

elements.quote: The literature search was conducted from inception up to 14 August 2020 by using predefined search terms... The last update was on 10 October 2020.
elements.reason: Search dates for all sources are explicitly reported, including the last update date.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), Web of Science (www.webofknowledge.com), Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) and the COVID19 Research Database (WHO)... from inception up to 14 August 2020
elements.reason: Four databases named with URLs/platforms and coverage dates (inception to 14 August 2020).

elements.quote: the COVID19 Research Database (WHO) (https://search.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov)... We did not apply any restrictions or filters.
elements.reason: The WHO COVID-19 research database (online repository) is named with URL and date coverage; no restrictions stated.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), Web of Science (www.webofknowledge.com), Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org)
elements.reason: Online sources are named with URLs.
No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies; authors were contacted only for missing data, not for study identification.
No individuals were contacted to identify studies.

elements.quote: Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews on this topic were screened for further relevant studies.
elements.reason: Types of reference lists examined are specified.

elements.quote: To identify studies that were published after the last update, we continuously searched PubMed using the e-mail alert service, which was based on our search terms described above. The last update was on 10 October 2020.
elements.reason: An ongoing PubMed e-mail alert service is described with the update date, but this is not formal backward/forward citation searching with a citation index/platform and explicit search date.
No journals or conference proceedings were handsearched or consulted as sources.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov), Web of Science (www.webofknowledge.com), Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) and the COVID19 Research Database (WHO) ... The literature search was conducted from inception up to 14 August 2020 by using predefined search terms (see electronic supplementary material (ESM) Table 1).
elements.reason: Databases, dates and continuous PubMed alert searching are reported, and the full search strategy is referenced to supplementary ESM Table 1, but the complete search strings are not reproduced in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We did not apply any restrictions or filters.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that no limits or filters were applied, which fully addresses the reporting of search limits.
No citation of published search approaches or filters, or description of adaptations, appears in the retrieved evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools for search term identification.
No mention of tools used to translate search strings between databases.
No description of any validation of the search strategy in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is reported.
No description of the conceptual structure of the search or its development is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The screening of the studies was performed by two independent researchers (AL, MN) ... Titles and abstracts were scanned according to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (see below) and potentially relevant full texts were assessed for eligibility.
elements.reason: The Methods state that two researchers screened titles/abstracts and full texts.

elements.quote: The screening of the studies was performed by two independent researchers (AL, MN)
elements.reason: Independence of the two screening reviewers is explicitly reported.

elements.quote: any discrepancies were resolved by discussion with two other researchers (CH, SS)
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution during screening is described.

elements.quote: We successfully contacted study authors and received missing data or corrections for implausible data [16, 17, 24 - 27] and, thus, no study had to be excluded due to missing data. As the authors of one report did not reply to our request [28], we assumed that in statistical analyses of continuous measures, the variable was investigated as per 1 unit increase.
elements.reason: Contacting study investigators is reported, but primarily for missing data/data extraction rather than specifically for confirming eligibility; applicability as eligibility confirmation is only partially addressed.
No evidence of translated abstracts or articles requiring translation; non-English articles were excluded (figure_6 flow diagram shows '2 Not in English' exclusions).
No automation tools are mentioned anywhere in the selection process; screening was done manually by two researchers.
No externally derived classifiers are reported.
No internally derived classifiers are reported.
No machine-learning prioritisation or stopping rules are reported.
No crowdsourcing platforms are reported.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records are reported.

elements.quote: Severity of COVID-19 was defined as a composite endpoint, including death, endotracheal intubation for mechanical ventilation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, ICU admission, multiple organ dysfunction or failure, or hospital admission.
elements.reason: The two outcomes (COVID-19-related death and severity) are defined, and exposure/phenotype domains are listed (general characteristics, diabetes-specific factors, comorbidities, laboratory parameters), but detailed definitions of outcome domains largely rely on ESM Table 2 and exposure domains are not formally defined in the main text.

No changes to the processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported.

elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes how missing or unclear study information was handled and states the assumption made for non-responding authors (continuous variables analysed as per 1 unit increase).

No evidence indicates that a specific tool was used to determine which data items to collect; data items were based on a pre-piloted extraction form, so this conditional requirement does not apply based on the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The tool includes the following six domains: study participation, study attrition, prognostic factor measurements, outcome measurements, study confounding and statistical analysis/reporting (see ESM Methods and ESM Table 3 for more details)

elements.quote: Risk of bias was low in n = 6 studies, moderate in n = 8 studies and high in n = 8 studies (ESM Fig. 1).

No adaptations to the QUIPS tool are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: by applying the validated Cochrane tool, Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) [29]
elements.reason: An existing validated tool (QUIPS) was used; no new tool was developed.

elements.quote: Three researchers (AL, MN, SS) independently assessed the risk of bias of included studies in pairs of two... Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (three, working in independent pairs), their independence, and the disagreement-resolution procedure (discussion) are reported.
No process for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators is described; author contact was only for missing data extraction, not risk of bias.

elements.quote: independently assessed the risk of bias of included studies in pairs of two by applying the validated Cochrane tool
elements.reason: Risk-of-bias assessment was performed manually by researchers; no automation tools are mentioned, so the requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: We calculated summary RRs (SRR) and 95% CIs using DerSimonian and Laird random effects models and I 2 statistic to assess statistical heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The Methods specify the effect measure (summary relative risk with 95% CI) used for the meta-analysed outcomes (death and severity), and results consistently report SRRs for each association.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g. small/moderate/large effect cutoffs) or their rationale are reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

The choice of the relative risk as effect measure is not explicitly justified in the retrieved evidence; only the statistical method (DerSimonian and Laird random effects) is described.
